These are five grave sins which, when committed, lead one to fall immediately, i.e., with no intermediate period, into the Avīci hell after death due to their severity. Usually five are enumerated: killing one’s mother, father, or an arhat ; causing dissension in the order of monks (the saṅgha); and deliberately causing a tathāgata ’s blood to flow. But the exact number of items varies in different lists from two or three to five (cf. BHSD, s.v. ānantarya ). (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh339)

This translates Sanskrit ārūpya­samāpatti (“attainment of formless absorptions”) or ārūpyāvacara­dhyāna in Transformation of Karma , which in Tibetan is usually translated as gzugs med pa’i snyoms par ’jug pa . The four states of imperturbability are (1) the sphere of infinite space ; (2) the sphere of infinite consciousness ; (3) the sphere of nothingness (literally, “the sphere in which there is not the slightest bit of anything present”); and (4) the sphere of neither mind nor no-mind . See also “ meditative absorption .” (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh339)

Literally “those who have gone to the afterlife.” A synonym or interlinear gloss for preta ; ghost in Transformation of Karma . Pretas are a class of sentient beings belonging to the “bad” or “ unfortunate rebirth destinies ” (Skt. apāya ); see “ animal .” In the commentary to the Petavatthu (the seventh book of the Khuddakanikāya of the Pāli Canon), the former term is explained as “having gone to the beyond or the afterlife” (Pāli paralokagata ), which is effectively the same as Sanskrit preta and Pāli peta ; departed, dead. The meaning of durāgata or dūraṃgama (“far-going,” “going here and there”) may refer to the belief that the ghosts of the deceased are able to move freely and quickly through space because they do not have physical bodies, and that the realm of the ghosts does not, in fact, exist in a fixed location but is everywhere. As the stories of the Petavatthu illustrate, the worlds of ghosts and humans often intertwine. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh339)

This is likely a pre-reform expression. We were unable to determine the exact meaning of this Tibetan expression, and we did not find it used elsewhere in either the Kangyur or the Tengyur. In the Dictionary of Old Tibetan Orthography (Tib. bod yig brda rnying tshig mdzod ) by rnam rgyal tshe ring (2001), we find the entry nyon mongs bzod ; one who endures hardship or suffering, as an older Tibetan expression for a monk or nun (Tib. dge slong gi ming ). Thus, one literal translation that we are proposing for this expression is “one who sustains (or endures) suffering (or hardship).” Comparison with similar contexts in related texts (Toh 338, 1.13 (F.278.ab)) and passim , i.e., where we find rab tu byung ba tshul dang ldan pa rnams etc. instead, suggests that the expression may be a collective term for those who have entered the path to liberation (Skt. āryapudgala ; Pāli ariyapuggala ) or for the Buddhist saṅgha generally. See also “ those who have entered the path of liberation .” (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh339)
Part of the Tibetan translation of a Skt. stock phrase for the expression of esteem. See glory , good reputation . (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh339)

The first of the four states of imperturbability . In the formless realm (Skt. ārūpyadhātu ), no bodies or materiality of any kind exist, only mind; rebirth there is the result of accomplishing four formless meditative absorptions (Skt. ārūpya­samāpatti ; five absorptions, i.e., if one includes the stage of Skt. saṃjñā-vedayita-nirodha or nirodhasamāpatti ). (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh339)
One of twenty or twenty-four so-called secondary mental defilements or afflictions. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh339)

The opposites of the ten nonvirtuous courses of action (as they occur in 1.63 ; note that only nine actions are listed): Abstaining from killing , stealing , leading an unchaste life , lying , divisive talk, [abusive language], trivial talk , greed , hatred, and wrong views . (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh339)

An ideal monarch or emperor who rules in accordance with the Dharma over the entire universe or large parts of it (whatever the spatial extent of the known universe at a given time is conceived to be). A world system can have only one universal monarch at one given time, just as it can have only one buddha. Like a buddha, a universal monarch possesses the thirty-two major marks of a great being (Skt. mahā­puruṣa­lakṣaṇa ), and in addition he possesses seven precious objects: his magical wheel or disc, an elephant, a horse, a wish-fulfilling gem, a queen, a treasurer, and a counselor. He rules on the basis of ten royal qualities (Skt. rājadharma ): generosity, ethical conduct, nonattachment, honesty, gentleness, austerity, non-anger, nonviolence, patience, and tolerance. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh339)

The tenth of the ten nonvirtuous actions ; also one of five commonly listed kinds of erroneous views, wrong view designates the disbelief in the doctrine of karma, i.e., rebirth and karmic punishment and reward as a consequence of one’s actions (i.e., cause and effect of actions ). (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh339)
The name of Maker of Joy when she becomes fully awakened after twenty-eight eons. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh205)
The name of the beggar woman who receives a prediction of future awakening from the Buddha in The City Beggar Woman . (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh205)

One of the principal śrāvaka disciples of the Buddha, paired with Śāriputra. He was renowned for his miraculous powers. His family clan was descended from Mudgala, hence his name Maudgalyā­yana, “the son of Mudgala’s descendants.” Respectfully referred to as Mahā­maudgalyā­yana, “Great Maudgalyāyana.” (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh205)

An interlocuter in The Dharma Council . One of the principal śrāvaka disciples of the Buddha, paired with Śāriputra . He was renowned for his miraculous powers . His family clan was descended from Mudgala, hence his name Maudgalyāyana, “the son of Mudgala’s descendants.” (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh238)
A close hearer disciple of the Buddha, reknowned for his miraculous powers. Also rendered here just as “ Maud­galyā­yana .” (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh231)

During the life of the Buddha, Śrāvastī was the capital city of the powerful kingdom of Kośala, ruled by King Prasenajit, who became a follower and patron of the Buddha. It was also the hometown of Anāthapiṇḍada, the wealthy patron who first invited the Buddha there, and then offered him a park known as Jetavana, Prince Jeta’s Grove, which became one of the first Buddhist monasteries. The Buddha is said to have spent about twenty-five rainy seasons with his disciples in Śrāvastī, thus it is named as the setting of numerous events and teachings. It is located in present-day Uttar Pradesh in northern India. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh205)
The universe of a thousand to the power of three, or one billion, world systems. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh205)
This refers to the gnosis or omniscience of the Buddha, the “All-Knowing” or “Omniscient” One. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh286)
Also translated here as “ without conceptual elaborations .” (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh145)
The dome-shaped assembly hall where Indra teaches the Dharma located on the southwest side of Mount Meru. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh145)
To invest something with meaning. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh56)

In its most general sense, this term refers to the state of freedom from suffering and cyclic existence, or saṃsāra, that is the goal of the Buddhist path. More specifically, the term may refer to a category of advanced meditative attainment such as those of the “eight liberations.” (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh145)
A jewel. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh145)

Daughter of Śākya Daṇḍadhara (more commonly Daṇḍapāṇi), sister of Iṣudhara and Aniruddha, she was the wife of Prince Siddhārtha and mother of his only child, Rāhula. After Prince Siddhārtha left his kingdom and attained awakening as the Buddha, she became his disciple and one of the first women to be ordained as a bhikṣunī. She attained the level of an arhat, a worthy one, endowed with the six superknowledges. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh145)
See “ five acts with immediate results .” (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh216)
The process of karma, afflictions of the mind, and suffering. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh216)

The set of seven precious materials or substances includes a range of precious metals and gems, but their exact list varies. The set often consists of gold, silver, beryl, crystal, red pearls, emeralds, and white coral, but may also contain lapis lazuli, ruby, sapphire, chrysoberyl, diamonds, etc. The term is frequently used in the sūtras to exemplify preciousness, wealth, and beauty, and can describe treasures, offering materials, or the features of architectural structures such as stūpas, palaces, thrones, etc. The set is also used to describe the beauty and prosperity of buddha realms and the realms of the gods. In other contexts, the term saptaratna can also refer to the seven precious possessions of a cakravartin or to a set of seven precious moral qualities. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh216)
In the context of the sūtras, it refers to the Hearer Vehicle, the Solitary Buddha Vehicle, and the Great Vehicle. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh216)
Having an association with a state of purity (particularly mental purity) and therefore not leading to further negativity and/or pain. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh216)

An ideal monarch or emperor who, as the result of the merit accumulated in previous lifetimes, rules over a vast realm in accordance with the Dharma. Such a monarch is called a cakravartin because he bears a wheel ( cakra ) that rolls ( vartate ) across the earth, bringing all lands and kingdoms under his power. The cakravartin conquers his territory without causing harm, and his activity causes beings to enter the path of wholesome actions. According to Vasubandhu’s Abhidharmakośa , just as with the buddhas, only one cakravartin appears in a world system at any given time. They are likewise endowed with the thirty-two major marks of a great being ( mahāpuruṣalakṣaṇa ), but a cakravartin’s marks are outshined by those of a buddha. They possess seven precious objects: the wheel, the elephant, the horse, the wish-fulfilling gem, the queen, the general, and the minister. An illustrative passage about the cakravartin and his possessions can be found in The Play in Full (Toh 95), 3.3 – 3.13 . Vasubandhu lists four types of cakravartins: (1) the cakravartin with a golden wheel ( suvarṇacakravartin ) rules over four continents and is invited by lesser kings to be their ruler; (2) the cakravartin with a silver wheel ( rūpyacakravartin ) rules over three continents and his opponents submit to him as he approaches; (3) the cakravartin with a copper wheel ( tāmracakravartin ) rules over two continents and his opponents submit themselves after preparing for battle; and (4) the cakravartin with an iron wheel ( ayaścakravartin ) rules over one continent and his opponents submit themselves after brandishing weapons. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh216)

Roughly synonymous with abhicāra ( assaulting ), this broad category of rites includes those ritual practices and magical acts that are used to curse, exorcise malevolent influences, deter, harm, and kill enemies, and otherwise engage in hostile activities directed towards human and nonhuman targets. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh726)
One of the five primary tathāgatas , he presides over the vajra family . (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh726)
One of the five primary tathāgatas , he presides over the karma family . (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh726)
Here the five are listed as gold, pearl , crystal , coral, and sapphire . (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh726)
One of the five primary tathāgatas , he presides over the jewel family . (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh726)
One of the five primary tathāgatas , he presides over the tathāgata family . (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh726)

Literally “heart,” this term means the heart essence or the essence of the deity and can refer to its mantra, mudrā, or maṇḍala. Here, it refers to the mantra. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh509)
A class of supernatural beings. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh591)
“White Umbrella Goddess,” a female Buddhist deity renowned for her power to avert or repel threats from supernatural beings, disease, and misfortune. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh591)
A city in ancient India, located on the Campā River. It was the capital of the Aṅga state, which was located east of Magadha. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh42)

g: Five Sets of One Hundred Thousand
d: (1) The long Prajñā­pāramitā ( Toh 8 ), which contains 100,000 ślokas; (2) the Mahā­pari­nirvāṇa ( Toh 119 – 120 ), which contains 100,000 testaments given by the Buddha at the time of his pari­nirvāṇa ; (3) the Ratna­kūṭa ( Toh 45–93 ), which contains 100,000 distinct names of the Buddha; (4) the Avataṃsaka ( Toh 44 ), which contains 100,000 aspirations; and (5) the Laṅkāvatāra ( Toh 107 – 108 ), which contains 100,000 discourses that are ways of subjugating the rākṣasas. These five sets of 100,000 features are also said to correspond to the Buddha’s body, speech, mind, qualities, and activities, respectively. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh122)
Literally the “truth of the highest meaning,” this is the knowledge that can only be directly realized, but not grasped conceptually. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1183)
The “truth of the highest meaning” that can only be directly realized, but not grasped conceptually. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1189)
A posture in which the right foot is extended forward and the left knee is slightly bent. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1183)
A system of code words and terms with symbolic meaning that are used in the higher tantras. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1183)
One of the five tathāgatas, he is located in the southern quarter of tantric maṇḍalas and presides over the karma family. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1183)
One of the secondary kṣetras. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1183)
Another name for Amitābha. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1183)
This name can be used for fear personified, or more generally for “terrifying” ( bhīṣaṇa ) deities such as Bhairava or Yama. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1183)
Another name of Śiva, possibly reflecting his being the lord of bhūtas. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1183)
This appears to be another term for the body of true nature ( svabhāvikakāya ). (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1183)
“Brahmin woman,” one of the five mudrās, representing the activity family in the Hevajra system. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1183)
Toh 424. A Yoginī tantra featuring a maṇḍala centered on a heruka-type deity. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1183)
The god of the moon, or the moon personified. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1183)
One of the pīlavas. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1183)

A class of tantra that is typically listed second in traditional doxographies. Classified between Kriyā and Yoga tantra, these tantras include features of deity yoga that are not present in the Kriyā Tantras, but that are not as fully evolved as in the Yoga Tantras. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1183)
One of the fifteen yoginīs that inhabit the thirty-two subtle channels. Also, one of the yoginīs in the maṇḍala of Nairātmyā. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1183)
The samādhi of the basic state that is free of causes. The term can also be understood as “unconditioned,” “signless,” “without characteristics,” etc. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1183)
The ultimate absence of marks and signs in perceived objects. One of the three gateways to liberation; the other two are emptiness and wishlessness. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1189)
“Place of delight.” A type of a sacred site. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1183)
Secondary conditions that contribute to the arising of a given result. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1183)
There are three primary features of conditioned phenomena: enduring ( sthiti ), deteriorating ( jarā ), and passing away ( vyaya ). (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1183)
A Buddhist goddess. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1183)
The name of a goddess. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh440)

This term covers a wide range of meanings—in general a female being, not necessarily benevolent, ranging from a powerful spirit to a retinue deity in a maṇḍala. In the sūtras and Kriyā tantras, they are typically female spirits of a lower order. In the higher tantras they are powerful, realized deities linked to the channels within the subtle body. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1183)
Deity yoga consists in visualizing oneself in the form of the deity, and identifying with that. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1183)
One of the kṣetras. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1183)
It is uncertain which deity this name refers to; possibly to Kubera. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1183)

The “body of qualities,” one of the three bodies of a buddha, acquired when the ultimate reality is realized and actualized. The other two bodies are sambhogakāya (“enjoyment body”) and nirmāṇakāya (“creation body”). (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1183)

In distinction to the rūpakāya, or form body of a buddha, this is the eternal imperceptible realization of a buddha. In origin it was a term for the presence of the Dharma, and has come to become synonymous with the true nature. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh116)

The ultimate nature or essence of the enlightened mind of the buddhas. It is said to be non-arising, free from the limits of conceptual elaboration, empty of inherent existence, naturally radiant, beyond duality, and spacious. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh507)

In distinction to the rūpakāya , or form body of a buddha, this is the eternal, imperceivable realization of a buddha. In origin it was a term for the presence of the Dharma and has become synonymous with the true nature. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh56)

Literally “source of phenomena.” this refers to the principle of creation represented, in its simplest form, by a (white) triangle pointing down. It is equated with the triangular area of the vagina. It can also have the form of two intersecting triangles and other more elaborate forms. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1183)
The fifth bodhisattva level. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1183)

One of the two main divisions of Jainism, the other one being the Śvetāmbara. As their names suggest, the Digāmbaras (“dressed in the directions”) go naked and the Śvetambāras (“attired in white”) wear white robes. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1183)
The third moment in sexual yoga, corresponding to the moment when pleasure subsides. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1183)

The third moment in sexual yoga, corresponding to the moment when pleasure subsides. According to Ratnākaraśānti, this moment corresponds to the joy of cessation. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1189)
The pride associated with confidently identifying oneself with the deity. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1183)
“Divine”; one of the subtle channels in the body. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1183)
“Divine,” one of the subtle channels in the body. According to Ratnākaraśānti, this channel is associated with the yoginī Gaurī. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1189)
One of the two goddesses that go by the name Gaurī. Her name means “door guardian.”s (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1183)
“Hateful”; one of the subtle channels in the body. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1183)
“Hateful,” one of the subtle channels in the body. According to Ratnākaraśānti, this channel is associated with the yoginī Pukkasī. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1189)

The eight charnel grounds or cemeteries associated with eight geographic locations in India, and, esoterically, with particular locations in the human body. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1183)

These are the progressively more subtle states of meditative attainment. Simplified, they could be summed up as follows: (1) one that consists in looking at external forms while perceiving ( sam + √ jñā ) form internally; (2) one that consists in looking at external forms without perceiving form internally; (3) the third one, in contradistinction to the first two, is the “pleasant” ( śubha ) liberation, established by cultivating the pleasant aspect of form; (4) where one dwells in the realization of the sphere of infinite space; (5) transcending the sphere of infinite space, where one dwells in the realization of the sphere of infinite consciousness; (6) transcending the sphere of infinite consciousness, where one dwells in the realization of the sphere of nothingness; (7) transcending the sphere of nothingness, where one dwells in the realization of the sphere of neither perception nor nonperception; and (8) transcending the sphere of neither perception and nonperception, where one dwells in the realization of the cessation of conception and feeling. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1183)

A series of progressively more subtle states of meditative realization or attainment. There are several presentations of these found in the canonical literature. One of the most common is as follows: (1) One observes form while the mind dwells at the level of the form realm. (2) One observes forms externally while discerning formlessness internally. (3) One dwells in the direct experience of the body’s pleasant aspect. (4) One dwells in the realization of the sphere of infinite space by transcending all conceptions of matter, resistance, and diversity. (5) Transcending the sphere of infinite space, one dwells in the realization of the sphere of infinite consciousness. (6) Transcending the sphere of infinite consciousness, one dwells in the realization of the sphere of nothingness. (7) Transcending the sphere of nothingness, one dwells in the realization of the sphere of neither perception nor nonperception. (8) Transcending the sphere of neither perception and nonperception, one dwells in the realization of the cessation of conception and feeling. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh94)
One of the four main ritual activities, this involves bringing a target under one’s influence. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1183)
The way phenomena are experienced indivisibly on the level of absolute truth. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1183)
The seventh bodhisattva level. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1183)
The first of the three yogas of the stage of arising. Generally, the first yoga involves the generation of the central maṇḍala deity and its consort. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1183)

An early sequence of yogas for generating the deity, they are particularly well developed in Yoga tantras. This procedure, as indicated by its name, entails the visualization of five aspects: (1) the row of vowels transforming into the moon; (2) the row of consonants transforming into the sun; (3) the seed syllable in between these transforming into the features of the deity; (4) the emanation of the mantra deities and reabsorption into the seed syllable; and (5) the full manifestation of the deity by means of the transformation of everything into one. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1183)
Also called the “five great elements” ( pañcamahābhūta ), these are the elements of earth, water, air, fire, and space. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1183)
See the entry for “five buddhas.” (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1183)
The four types of activity ( karman ), or the four types of rites ( karman ), are pacifying, nourishing, enthralling, and hostility. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1183)
One of the goddesses who offers the articles of worship. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1183)

Normally a title of respect for a bodhisattva or other realized being, it has a range of esoteric meanings in the Hevajra Tantra . When used in juxtaposition with vajrasattva and samayasattva , it refers to the enjoyment body. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1183)
One of the epithets of Hevajra. The citta in his name could be a short form of bodhicitta, which is equated with semen. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1183)

One of the epithets of Hevajra. The citta in his name could be a short form of bodhicitta, which is equated with semen.According to Ratnākaraśānti, he embodies the nature of great joy. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1189)
Any of the principal five elements: earth, water, fire, air, and space. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1183)

The second of the three vehicles in the scheme of Foundational Vehicle ( hīnayāna ), Great Vehicle, and Vajra Vehicle ( vajrayāna ). Another scheme of the three vehicles distinguishes them into the Vehicle of Śrāvakas ( śrāvakayāna ), Vehicle of Pratyekabuddhas ( pratyeka­buddha­yāna ), and the Great Vehicle. In this scheme, the Great Vehicle is further divided into the way of the perfections ( pāramitānaya ), the “method of perfections,” and the way of mantra ( mantranaya ). (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1183)
One of the chandohas. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1183)

A wrathful deity representing buddhahood itself, one of the most prominent in the system of the Yoginī tantras. There are three forms of Hevajra with two, six, and sixteen arms. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1183)
One of the secondary kṣetras. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1183)
“Happy countenance”; one of the subtle channels in the body. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1183)
“Happy countenance,” one of the subtle channels in the body. According to Ratnākaraśānti, this channel is associated with the yoginī Ḍombinī. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1189)

One of the principal Vedic gods who also appears frequently in Buddhist literature, often under the name Śakra. In Buddhist cosmology he rules over the Heaven of the Thirty-Three. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1183)

The ritual process of being introduced to and authorized in the practice of specific deities, maṇḍalas, and yogas. The term literally means “sprinkling” or “anointing,” and is modeled on rites of royal investiture. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1183)

The “innate” or natural state of mind that is always there but remains unrecognized for as long as duality prevails. This state can be recognized during the innate joy ( sahajānanda ) experienced during the sexual yoga. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1183)

The “innate” or natural state of mind that is always there but remains unrecognized for as long as duality prevails. This state can be recognized during the innate joy ( sahajānanda ) experienced during sexual yoga. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1189)

The fourth of the four joys. Although referred to as the “fourth,” it is meant to be discerned at the end of the supreme joy and the onset of the joy of cessation. This joy characterizes the innate state. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1183)

The fourth of the four joys . Although referred to as the “fourth,” it is meant to be discerned at the end of the supreme joy and the onset of the joy of cessation. This joy characterizes the innate state. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh417)
The yoga that employs the subtle channels and cakras. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1183)
The period between death and rebirth. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1183)
Another name of Varuṇa. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1183)
One of the pīṭhas. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1183)
In the Jaina philosophy, jīva is an independently existing individual being. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1183)
The first of the four joys; it corresponds to the period in sexual yoga up to the onset of climax. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1183)
The first of the four joys ; it corresponds to the period in sexual yoga up to the onset of climax. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh417)
The third of the four joys; it corresponds to the period in sexual yoga immediately after the climax. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1183)
The third of the four joys ; it corresponds to the period in sexual yoga immediately after the climax. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh417)
A code word for female genitalia. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1183)
One of the secondary chandohas. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1183)
One of the pīṭhas. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1183)
One of the kṣetras. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1183)
One of the kṣetras. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1183)

A staff or spear with skulls or human heads impaled on its shaft. It is typically wielded by deities in their more fearsome aspects. In the Hevajra practice of the sole hero , the khaṭvāṅga represents the consort Nairātmyā. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1183)
One of the fifteen yoginīs that inhabit the thirty-two subtle channels. Also, the name of a yoginī in the maṇḍala of Nairātmyā. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1183)
The ritual act of taking life. It falls under the category of hostile rites ( abhicāra ) among the four ritual activities. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1183)
One of the secondary chandohas. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1183)
One of the pīṭhas. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1183)
One of the pīṭhas, also called Pullīramalaya. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1189)

A class of tantric scripture that generally features elaborate rites directed toward both mundane goals‍—such as health, prosperity, and protection‍—and to the ultimate goal of liberation. The Mañjuśrīmūlakalpa and Amoghapāśakalparāja exemplify this class of tantra. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1183)
A yakṣa who is regarded as the lord of wealth and the guardian of the northern quarter. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1183)
One of the secondary kṣetras. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1183)
A code word for sexual intercourse. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1183)
“Born from a tortoise”; one of the subtle channels in the body. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1183)

A female Buddhist deity with the specific power to enthrall. She is typically portrayed shooting the arrows of love from a bow made of flowers. She is also popular in some Śākta cults. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1183)
One of the chandohas. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1183)
The radiant state of awareness that is free from duality. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1183)
A variation of the name of the Mahāsāṅghika, one of the four main congregations. They split from the Sthaviravāda during the Second Council. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1183)
One of the secondary pīṭhas. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1183)
The consort of the tathāgata Ratneśa. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1183)
“Destroyer of Māra”; one of the subtle channels in the body. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1183)
“Vajra Jealousy,” one of the six emanations of Nairātmyā that correspond to the six sense faculties and the six mental poisons. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1183)
A concept in the Yogācāra system indicating their position that perceived phenomena do not exist independently of the mind that perceives them. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1183)
The view that presumes that nothing is external to consciousness in the ontological sense. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1189)
One of the five wisdoms . This is the nature of mind that reflects phenomena exactly as they are, without any distortion due to conceptuality. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1183)
“Vajra Delusion,” one of the six emanations of Hevajra that correspond to the six sense faculties and six mental poisons. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1183)
One of the kṣetras. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1183)
One of the secondary pīṭhas, said to be the same as Pāṭaliputra. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1183)

A concept of Great Vehicle Buddhism referring to the state of nirvāṇa that can be attained while still in the physical body. The implication is that this type of nirvāṇa is not a fixed ( pratiṣṭhita ) condition of abiding in an inactive state. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1183)
Mental obscurations caused by the afflictions. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1183)
Mental obscurations caused by the afflictive emotions. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1189)
One of the pīṭhas. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1183)

The person who recites the content of a Buddhist sūtra, tantra, or other scriptural work, thereby recounting the event for later audiences. Typically, they do so with the rejoinder that is being recited just as it was originally heard. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1183)
“Lotus Lord of the Dance,” Avalokiteśvara in the form of a heruka. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1183)
Another name of Pāṇḍurā. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1183)
A ritual activity falling under the category of hostile rites ( abhicāra ). (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1183)

The “System of Perfections” is another name for the Great Vehicle that is used to differentiate the exoteric teaching of the Great Vehicle from the esoteric, tantric teaching preserved in the “System of Mantra” ( mantranaya ), also known as the Vajrayāna. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1183)
A Buddhist goddess who typically takes the form of a piśācī. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1183)
A city in ancient India, now Patna, Bihar. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1183)
One of the pīṭhas, also called Pullīramalaya. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1183)
“Purifier”; one of the subtle channels in the body. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1183)
A name of Hevajra. Picu is cotton wool or tufts of grass, i.e. something soft and delicate, and vajra is something infinitely hard. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1183)
“Vajra Spite,” one of the six emanations of Hevajra that correspond to the to the six sense faculties and the six mental poisons. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1183)
The visualized process of assigning and placing syllables in various body parts. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1183)
Another name of Nairātmyā. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1183)
“Loving”; one of the subtle channels in the body. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1183)
“Joy,” an epithet of Nairātmyā. Prīti is also one of the two wives of Kāmadeva. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1183)
The provisional meaning as opposed to the definitive meaning ( nītārtha ). (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1183)

Another name for the Sammatīya school. The name pudgalavāda , “the doctrine of pudgala,” indicates the belief in a pudgala , a discrete and enduring identity or individuality within beings. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1183)
“Washerwoman,” she is one the five mudrās, representing the activity family in the Hevajra system. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1183)
Another name of Nairṛti. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1183)
One of the apsarases. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1183)
One of the offering goddesses. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1183)
One of the fifteen yoginīs that inhabit the thirty-two subtle channels. Also, the name of a yoginī in the maṇḍala of Nairātmyā. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1183)

An alternative name for Indra, lord of the gods, who appears frequently in Buddhist literature. According to Buddhist cosmology, he resides in the Heaven of the Thirty-Three. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1183)

A specific system for the stage of arising. It consists of three stages: first yoga ( ādiyoga ), the supreme ruler of the maṇḍala ( maṇḍalarājāgrī ), and the supreme ruler of activity ( karmarājāgrī ). (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1183)
The form of Tārā associated with the activity of enthralling. The consort of the tathāgata Amoghasiddhi. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1183)
A variation on the name of the Sāmmitiyās, one of the four main congregations. One of the offshoots of the Vātsīputrīya. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1183)
A variation of the name of the Sammitīyas, one of the four main congregations. One of the offshoots of the Vātsīputrīya. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1189)
“Variegated,” one of the subtle channels in the body. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1183)
“Variegated,” one of the subtle channels in the body. According to Ratnākaraśānti, this channel is associated with the yoginī Śabarī. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1189)
A short form of Vajrasattva. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1183)
One of the chandohas. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1183)

A term denoting the distinct Buddhist ordination lineages, and by extension the Vinaya, Abhidhārma, and Sūtra collections central to them. Traditionally there were said to be as many as eighteen separate nikāyas . In the Hevajra Tantra four are mentioned: the Sthaviravāda (Theravāda), Sarvāstivāda, Sammatīya, and Mahāsāṅghika. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1183)

In the context of the Hevajra Tantra , the name seems to refer to the Śaiva-Siddhānta, “the established conclusion of Shaivism,” a school of thought and ritual practice based on twenty-eight Śaiva āgamas or tantras, authoritative scriptures in Sanskrit that proclaim their origins as divine knowledge revealed by Shiva (source: Oxford Bibliographies ). (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1183)
A type of hostile rite ( abhicāra ). (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1183)
A variation of the name of the Sthaviravādins, one of the four main congregations. They split from the Mahāsaṅghika during the Second Council. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1183)

A variation of the name of the Sthaviravādins (Theravādins), one of the four main congregations. They split from the Mahāsaṅghika during the Second Council. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1189)

Generally, a term for the maṇḍala wherein the deities, as the “supported maṇḍala” ( ādheyamaṇḍala ), reside. In the visualization process, this term may also refer to one’s own body as the dwelling place of the deity or deities. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1183)

This term refers to the circle of the deities abiding in the “support maṇḍala.” In the visualization process, this term can also refer to the subtle channels in one’s own body personified as deities. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1183)
The third of the three yogas of the stage of arising. The supreme ruler of activity involves the activities of the deities once they have been generated. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1183)

The second of the three yogas of the stage of arising. The supreme ruler of the maṇḍala involves the emanation of the remaining maṇḍala deities from the original pair. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1183)

The second of the three yogas of the generation stage. The supreme ruler of the maṇḍala involves the emanation of the remaining maṇḍala deities from the original pair. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1189)
The god of the sun, or the sun personified. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1183)
One of the secondary chandohas. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1183)

The “body of true nature,” a mode of embodiment of awakened beings, this is understood to represent the inseparable union of the other three buddha bodies: the nirmāṇakāya, sambhogakāya, and dharmakāya. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1183)

g: The Dhāraṇī of the Six Gates
d: Toh 141 . A text that Kāṇha lists among works associated with the Sautrāntika tradition. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1183)
Toh 141 . A text that Ratnākaraśānti lists among works associated with the Sautrāntika tradition. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1189)
Toh 324 . A text that Kāṇha lists among works associated with the Sautrāntika tradition. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1183)
Toh 1095 . A text that Kāṇha lists among works associated with the Sautrāntika tradition. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1183)
Toh 1095 . A text that Ratnākaraśānti lists among works associated with the Sautrāntika tradition. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1189)
Toh 323 . A text that Kāṇha lists among works associated with the Sautrāntika tradition. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1183)
Toh 323 . A text that Ratnākaraśānti lists among works associated with the Sautrāntika tradition. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1189)
Another name of Amitābha, one of the five tathāgatas. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1183)
Another name of Agni, the god of fire. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1183)
One of the fifteen yoginīs that inhabit the thirty-two subtle channels. Also, one of the yoginīs in the maṇḍala of Nairātmyā. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1183)
The deity who delivers the Hevajra Tantra . In the Hevajra Tantra this name is interchangeable with Vajrasattva. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1183)

Vajradhara is the deity who delivers the Hevajra Tantra . As a deity, he seems to be the same as Vajrasattva. According to the Muktāvalī on Hevajra Tantra 1.1.2, Vajradhara is the body, speech, and mind of all tathāgatas. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1189)
Another name of Vajrayāna. The equivalent Tibetan term typically translates vajrayāna . (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1183)
One of the fifteen yoginīs that inhabit the thirty-two subtle channels. Also, another name of Vāriyoginī. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1183)
The first moment in sexual yoga that consists in embracing, kissing, etc. This moment is associated with the first joy. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1183)
The name of a deity. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh358)
Vārī, one of the yoginīs in the maṇḍala of Nairātmyā. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1183)
One of the yoginīs in the maṇḍala of Nairātmyā. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1189)
The god of wind. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1183)
These are the followers of the Vedānta system, first expounded in the Upaniṣads. One of the six main philosophical systems of India. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1183)
One of the pīlavas, and a mountain range in central India. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1183)

Also called mantranīti (“mantra system”) this term broadly refers to the tantric schools of Buddhism. Together with the pāramitānaya (or pāramitānīti ), the way of the perfections, the way of mantra forms part of the Great Vehicle when the “three vehicles” are counted as the Vehicle of Śrāvakas ( śrāvakayāna ), the Vehicle of Pratyekabuddhas ( pratyeka­buddha­yāna ), and the Great Vehicle ( mahāyāna ). When the three vehicles are enumerated as the Foundational Vehicle ( hīnayāna ), Great Vehicle, and Vajra Vehicle ( vajrayāna ), the way of mantra specifically refers to the latter. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1183)

Also called mantranīti (“mantra system”), this term broadly refers to the tantric schools of Buddhism. Together with the pāramitānaya (or pāramitānīti ), the way of the perfections, the way of mantra forms part of the Great Vehicle when the “three vehicles” are counted as the Vehicle of Śrāvakas ( śrāvakayāna ), the Vehicle of Pratyekabuddhas ( pratyeka­buddhayāna ), and the Great Vehicle ( mahāyāna ). When the three vehicles are enumerated as the Foundational Vehicle ( hīnayāna ), Great Vehicle, and Vajra Vehicle ( vajrayāna ), the way of mantra specifically refers to the latter. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1189)
A synonym of Mantranaya, the “mantra system” that later became known as Vajranaya or Vajrayāna. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1183)
One of the five wisdoms . As the name suggests, this wisdom makes the activity of the buddhas unfailing and always accomplishing the benefit of beings. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1183)
One of the five wisdoms . This wisdom apprehends distinct qualities of phenomena in their infinity, clearly perceiving each phenomenon as distinct. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1183)
One of the five wisdoms . This is the wisdom that regards all beings with equal love and compassion, without differentiating between friend and foe. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1183)
One of the five wisdoms . This omniscient wisdom knows reality according to the absolute truth. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1183)
The name of the third of the four initiations, this involves union with a consort, who is identified by the term prajñā . (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1183)
This term refers to the dualistic mind that responds to the stimuli of objects, or to the samādhi techniques whereby the mind focuses on objects. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1183)
Another name of Kubera. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1183)
The god of the realm of the dead and the guardian of the southern quarter. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1183)

The highest class of tantra in many traditional doxographies, this class of tantric scripture includes the tantras also known as Yoginī tantras, such as the Cakraśaṃvara Tantra and Hevajra Tantra . (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1183)

A class of Buddhist tantra focused upon the figure of the yoginī and the meditative manipulation of the subtle energetic anatomy of the physical body. This genre is typified by the Hevajratantra , Cakrasaṃvara­tantra , and Mahāmāyātantra . (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1183)

The penultimate class of tantra in many traditional doxographies, this class of tantric scripture includes the tantras also known as Mahāyoga tantras, such as the Guhyasamāja Tantra . (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1183)
Sons of the goddess Diti. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh609)

In Indian mythology, the garuḍa is an eagle-like bird that is regarded as the king of all birds, normally depicted with a sharp, owl-like beak, often holding a snake, and with large and powerful wings. They are traditionally enemies of the nāgas. In the Vedas, they are said to have brought nectar from the heavens to earth. Garuḍa can also be used as a proper name for a king of such creatures. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh609)

Morally virtuous or disciplined conduct and the abandonment of morally undisciplined conduct of body, speech, and mind. In a general sense, moral discipline is the cause for rebirth in higher, more favorable states, but it is also foundational to Buddhist practice as one of the three trainings ( triśikṣā ) and one of the six perfections of a bodhisattva. Often rendered as “ethics,” “discipline,” and “morality.” (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh329)
See n.314 for this term in the translation. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh467)
“Subsequent yoga ,” the second of four stages in the practice of Black Yamāri . (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh467)
A class of celestial female beings known for their great beauty. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh467)
Ficus religiosa , the “bodhi tree.” (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh467)
Ficus religiosa , the species of fig tree under which the Buddha attained awakening. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh485)
“Highest yoga ,” the third of four stages in the practice of Black Yamāri . (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh467)
An epithet of Kāmadeva or Vajrānaṅga . (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh467)
Tentatively, the line that demarcates the outer circumference of the maṇḍala palace. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh467)

In this text, it mostly refers to the female sexual and reproductive organs. However, this term encompasses several meanings, including “good fortune,” “happiness,” and “majesty.” It forms the root of the word bhagavat ( Blessed One). A number of Buddhist esoteric scriptures are set within the bhaga of a female deity from the Buddhist pantheon. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh467)
The principal deity of this tantra. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh467)
A deity in Vajraḍākinī ’s maṇḍala. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh467)
Toponym of an unidentified place. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh467)
A deity in the maṇḍala of Black Yamāri . (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh467)
A deity in Ekajaṭā ’s maṇḍala. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh467)
An ornament of the maṇḍala palace. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh467)

Used as an adjective, the term sampuṭa indicates two bowls, skull cups , etc. that are joined at the mouth to form an enclosed interior space. As a noun, sampuṭa can refer to an earthenware bowl or to the sphere created by conjoined bowls. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh467)

Aa ritual implement that looks like two crossed vajras with a common sphere in the center. This implement is also known as a viśvavajra in Sanskrit and sna tshogs rdo rje in Tibetan. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh467)
In the Tantra of Back Yamāri , the first in a series of four initiations . (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh467)
One sixtieth of a sidereal day, which roughly corresponds to a period of twenty four hours ( ahorātra ). (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh467)
“Cudgel Yamāri ,” A deity in the maṇḍala of Black Yamāri . (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh467)
A tooth-stick, a small piece of wood which is chewed for cleaning one’s teeth. In the Tantra of Black Yamāri this represents the syllable da . (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh467)
A Tibetan monk and translator; identified as an editor / reviser of The Tantra of Black Yamāri . (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh467)
Epithet of Kāmadeva or Vajrānaṅga . (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh467)
Datura metel . (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh467)
“Intense seeds,” a term for the seeds of Datura metel . (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh467)
Name of a yakṣiṇī in the maṇḍala of Ekajaṭā . (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh467)
A goddess in the maṇḍala of Heruka . (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh467)
The offering goddess of incense. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh467)
The deities who are visualized standing in and thus guarding the doors of a given maṇḍala. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh467)

The accomplished translator and tantric master Ra Lotsāwa Dorjé Drakpa (rwa lo tsA ba rdo rje grags pa, c. 1016–1128) who is credited with having established the dmar nag ’jigs gsum “The three [cycles] of red [ Yamāri ], black [ Yamāri ], and [Vajra-]Terrifier,” and particularly the third, in Tibet. Ralo, as he is often called, was notorious as a tantric sorcerer who used black magic and his yogic powers attained through Vajrabhairava practice to overcome and even kill some of his opponents. His biography, written by his grandnephew Ra Yeshé Sengé (rwa ye shes seng ge), flourished c. 1150 ᴄᴇ ), is translated in Cuevas 2015. The colophon of The Tantra of Black Yamāri dates that he was the editor who last revised the translation from Sanskrit. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh467)
“Hatred Yamāri ,” a deity in the maṇḍala of Black Yamāri . Also known as Yamāri Dveṣavajra . (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh467)
In the Tantra of Back Yamāri , the fourth in a series of four initiations . (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh467)
The term conveys the notions of transferring authority, power, or control to a person or object. The term can in some contexts be translated as “blessing.” (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh467)
A ritual activity for bringing human and non-human beings under one’s control, for a variety of purposes; one of the four main ritual activities. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh467)
The name of a meditative absorption . (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh467)
The name of a meditative absorption . (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh467)
The name of a siddhi . (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh467)
A deity in the maṇḍala of Black Yamāri . (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh467)
A yakṣiṇī in Ekajaṭā ’s maṇḍala. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh467)
An offering goddess. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh467)
“Song,” a goddess from the set of offering goddesses who often appear in sets of four or eight in maṇḍala assemblies. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh485)
Blue dye extracted from the Indigo plant. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh467)
“Jealousy Yamāri ,” a deity in the maṇḍala of Black Yamāri . Also known as Īrṣyāvajra Yamāri Īrṣyāvajra (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh467)
A deity in Ekajaṭā ’s maṇḍala. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh467)

One of the first Buddhist monasteries, located in a park outside Śrāvastī, the capital of the ancient kingdom of Kośala in northern India. This park was originally owned by Prince Jeta, hence the name Jetavana, meaning Jeta’s grove. The wealthy merchant Anāthapiṇḍada, wishing to offer it to the Buddha, sought to buy it from him, but the prince, not wishing to sell, said he would only do so if Anāthapiṇḍada covered the entire property with gold coins. Anāthapiṇḍada agreed, and managed to cover all of the park except the entrance, hence the name Anāthapiṇḍadasyārāmaḥ, meaning Anāthapiṇḍada’s park. The place is usually referred to in the sūtras as “Jetavana, Anāthapiṇḍada’s park,” and according to the Saṃghabhedavastu the Buddha used Prince Jeta’s name in first place because that was Prince Jeta’s own unspoken wish while Anāthapiṇḍada was offering the park. Inspired by the occasion and the Buddha’s use of his name, Prince Jeta then offered the rest of the property and had an entrance gate built. The Buddha specifically instructed those who recite the sūtras to use Prince Jeta’s name in first place to commemorate the mutual effort of both benefactors. Anāthapiṇḍada built residences for the monks, to house them during the monsoon season, thus creating the first Buddhist monastery. It was one of the Buddha’s main residences, where he spent around nineteen rainy season retreats, and it was therefore the setting for many of the Buddha’s discourses and events. According to the travel accounts of Chinese monks, it was still in use as a Buddhist monastery in the early fifth century ᴄᴇ , but by the sixth century it had been reduced to ruins. A major śrāvaka disciple and personal attendant of the Buddha Śākyamuni during the last twenty-five years of his life. He was a cousin of the Buddha (according to the Mahāvastu , he was a son of Śuklodana, one of the brothers of King Śuddhodana, which means he was a brother of Devadatta; other sources say he was a son of Amṛtodana, another brother of King Śuddhodana, which means he would have been a brother of Aniruddha). Ānanda, having always been in the Buddha’s presence, is said to have memorized all the teachings he heard and is celebrated for having recited all the Buddha’s teachings by memory at the first council of the Buddhist saṅgha, thus preserving the teachings after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa. The phrase “Thus did I hear at one time,” found at the beginning of the sūtras, usually stands for his recitation of the teachings. He became a patriarch after the passing of Mahākāśyapa. The Mūlasarvāstivādin tradition grouped the Buddha’s early sūtra discourses into four divisions, or āgama (Tib. mdo sde’i lung sde bzhi ): the Dīrghāgama (Tib. lung ring po ), the Madhyamāgama (Tib. lung bar ma ), the Ekottarikāgama (Tib. lung gcig las ’phros pa ), and the Saṃyuktāgama (Tib. lung dag ldan / yang dar par ldan pa’i lung ). They are more familiar to many English-speaking Buddhists through the translations of their Pali correlates: the Dīgha Nikāya, Majjhima Nikāya, Aṅguttara Nikāya, and the Samyutta Nikāya, for which see the Wisdom Publications titles: The Long Discourses of the Buddha, The Middle-Length Discourses of the Buddha, The Numerical Discourses of the Buddha, and The Connected Discourses of the Buddha, respectively. The Sanskrit Chapter on Leather gives this location first in the probably erroneous form aśmakana­garāntaka (Tib. F.251.b rdo can zhes bya ba’i yul gyi mtha’ na ), or “border town of Aśma.” In the second case, the probably correct Sanskrit reads aśmāparāntakeṣu jana­padeṣu or “in the frontier land of Aśma” (the Tibetan translation is identical to the previous instance: rdo can zhes bya ba’i yul gyi mtha’ na ). According to Edgerton, the Skt. aparāntaka (p. 44, col. 2) can refer specifically to the country of Aparānta or more generally to the western border (i.e., in present-day Maharashtra). In his translation of the parallel passages in the Divyāvadāna , Rotman (2008: p. 392, n. 85) gives “region of Aśmāparāntaka,” which he explains to be a conjunct of Aparānta (as in “the country of…”) and Aśma (a.k.a. Aśmaka, Aśvaka, Pali Assaka, the latter of which is also in present-day Maharashtra). The Tibetan translation supports Rotman’s suggestion to take Aśma to be the name of a specific region in the western lands, rendered in Tibetan as rdo can . Thus, here, we have elected to translate this phrase in both instances as “the frontier country of Aśmaka.” (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1-5)

In Buddhist cosmology, the Heaven of the Thirty-Three is the second lowest of the six heavens in the desire realm ( kāmadhātu ). Situated on the flat summit of Mount Sumeru, it lies above the Heaven of the Four Great Kings ( Caturmahārāja­kāyika ) and below the Yāma Heaven. It consists of thirty-three regions, each presided by one of thirty-three chief gods, and the overall ruler is Śakra. The presiding gods are divided into four groups named in the Abhidharma­kośa­ṭīkā (Toh 4092): the eight gods of wealth, two Aśvin youths, eleven fierce ones, and twelve suns. The thirty-three regions themselves are enumerated and described in The Application of Mindfulness of the Sacred Dharma , Toh 287, 4.B.2 et seq.). (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1-5)

A frequently used synonym for buddha . According to different explanations, it can be read as tathā-gata , literally meaning “one who has thus gone,” or as tathā-āgata , “one who has thus come.” Gata , though literally meaning “gone,” is a past passive participle used to describe a state or condition of existence. Tatha­(tā) , often rendered as “suchness” or “thusness,” is the quality or condition of things as they really are, which cannot be conveyed in conceptual, dualistic terms. Therefore, this epithet is interpreted in different ways, but in general it implies one who has departed in the wake of the buddhas of the past, or one who has manifested the supreme awakening dependent on the reality that does not abide in the two extremes of existence and quiescence. It is also often used as a specific epithet of the Buddha Śākyamuni. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh324)

The term bhikṣu , often translated as “monk,” refers to the highest among the eight types of prātimokṣa vows that make one part of the Buddhist assembly. The Sanskrit term literally means “beggar” or “mendicant,” referring to the fact that Buddhist monks and nuns‍—like other ascetics of the time‍—subsisted on alms ( bhikṣā ) begged from the laity. In the Tibetan tradition, which follows the Mūlasarvāstivāda Vinaya, a monk follows 253 rules as part of his moral discipline. A nun ( bhikṣuṇī ; dge slong ma ) follows 364 rules. A novice monk ( śrāmaṇera ; dge tshul ) or nun ( śrāmaṇerikā ; dge tshul ma ) follows thirty-six rules of moral discipline (although in other vinaya traditions novices typically follow only ten). (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh762)

A type of nonhuman being whose precise status is subject to different views, but is included as one of the six classes of beings in the sixfold classification of realms of rebirth. In the Buddhist context, asuras are powerful beings said to be dominated by envy, ambition, and hostility. They are also known in the pre-Buddhist and pre-Vedic mythologies of India and Iran, and feature prominently in Vedic and post-Vedic Brahmanical mythology, as well as in the Buddhist tradition. In these traditions, asuras are often described as being engaged in interminable conflict with the devas (gods). (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh642)

g: Abhirati, the Pure Land of Akṣobhya Buddha

d: A class of generally benevolent nonhuman beings who inhabit the skies, sometimes said to inhabit fantastic cities in the clouds, and more specifically to dwell on the eastern slopes of Mount Meru, where they are ruled by the Great King Dhṛtarāṣṭra. They are most renowned as celestial musicians who serve the gods. In the Abhidharma, the term is also used to refer to the mental body assumed by sentient beings during the intermediate state between death and rebirth. Gandharvas are said to live on fragrances ( gandha ) in the desire realm, hence the Tibetan translation dri za , meaning “scent eater.” (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh510)

Śāntarakṣita (725-788) was an Indian Buddhist monk, scholar, and author who played a pivotal role in the introduction of Buddhism to Tibet. At the invitation of King Tri Songdetsen, he traveled to Tibet and assisted in the foundation of Samyé Monastery, presided over the ordination of the first Tibetan monks, and established a system of scholastic education modelled on the great monastic universities of Nālandā and Vikramaśīla. His philosophical writings were among the most influential in late Indian Buddhism. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh660)

One of the principal śrāvaka disciples of the Buddha, he was renowned for his discipline and for having been praised by the Buddha as foremost of the wise (often paired with Maudgalyā­yana, who was praised as foremost in the capacity for miraculous powers). His father, Tiṣya, to honor Śāriputra’s mother, Śārikā, named him Śāradvatīputra, or, in its contracted form, Śāriputra, meaning “Śārikā’s Son.” (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh238)

During the life of the Buddha, Śrāvastī was the capital city of the powerful kingdom of Kośala, ruled by King Prasenajit, who became a follower and patron of the Buddha. It was also the hometown of Anāthapiṇḍada, the wealthy patron who first invited the Buddha there, and then offered him a park known as Jetavana, Prince Jeta’s Grove, which became one of the first Buddhist monasteries. The Buddha is said to have spent about twenty-five rainy seasons with his disciples in Śrāvastī, thus it is named as the setting of numerous events and teachings. It is located in present-day Uttar Pradesh in northern India. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh199)

A tuft or protuberance on the head. It may refer to the uṣṇīṣa , a coif of flesh or hair atop a buddha’s head. This Tibetan expression can also translate śikhābandha, a topknot of hair. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh199)

Generally, they consist of abstaining from killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, lying, using intoxicants, eating after noon, wearing adornments, and sleeping on high beds. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1189)

“Sprinkling,” one of the subtle channels in the body. According to Ratnākaraśānti, this channel is associated with the yoginī Vajraḍākī. (From: https://84000.co/translation/toh1189)
